title: The Director of Vikram Just Picked Up the Gun Himself
excerpt: Lokesh Kanagaraj makes his acting debut as a gangster Devdas in DC — directed by Arun Matheswaran, scored by Anirudh, trailer-premiered at Cannes. Tamil cinema's busiest man just found a new job.
body:
There is a particular kind of audacity that comes from being the most in-demand filmmaker in Indian cinema and deciding, mid-reign, that you'd also like to try acting. **Lokesh Kanagaraj** — the architect of the Lokesh Cinematic Universe, the man who directed **Vikram**, **Leo**, and the upcoming **Coolie** — has done exactly that. His debut in front of the camera arrives on July 31 in **DC**, a gritty romantic action film that reimagines the classic Devdas as a love story told through gunpowder and black-and-white violence.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=2kntxizQIFI</youtube>

And the trailer? It premiered at **Cannes**. Just casually.

**DC** — short for Devadas and Chandra — is directed by **Arun Matheswaran**, who made the visually ravishing **Captain Miller** with Dhanush. The film is backed by **Sun Pictures**, scored by **Anirudh Ravichander** (because of course it is — the man scores everything that matters in Tamil cinema right now), and it co-stars **Wamiqa Gabbi** fresh off her breakout turns in **Bhooth Bangla** and the hit **Pati Patni Aur Woh Do**.

The setup is wickedly simple. Lokesh plays Devadas — not the tragic, pining lover of Sarat Chandra Chattopadhyay's 1917 novel, but a gangster on the run. Wamiqa's Chandra is no wilting ingenue either — she's fleeing her own mess. Their paths collide, and Devadas reluctantly becomes her protector. Love follows. Violence follows faster.



> **"I found a lot of similarities between Aamir sir and Kamal sir," Lokesh told The Hollywood Reporter India."**


From the trailer, Matheswaran's signature visual palette is unmistakable: desaturated frames cracking open into bursts of colour, bone-crunching action sequences choreographed by PC Stunts, and a camera that lingers on faces long enough to make you uncomfortable. The director has never been subtle, and with Lokesh as his lead, he doesn't need to be. There's a magnetic stillness to Lokesh on screen — the same quiet intensity that comes through in interviews, now aimed directly at a camera with Anirudh's score humming underneath it.

> "Devadas and Chandra are ready to light up the big screen!" the makers wrote, unveiling a poster that looked more Tarantino than Tagore.

**Sanjana Krishnamoorthy** rounds out the love triangle as Parvathi — the third corner that every Devdas retelling demands. Mukesh G handles cinematography, and GK Prasanna edits. The DNA is impeccable.

## Why Diaspora Audiences Should Be Watching

Lokesh Kanagaraj is, at this point, the closest thing Tamil cinema has to a brand name that transcends language barriers. The LCU — spanning Kaithi, Vikram, Leo, and the upcoming Coolie — has built a passionate global fanbase, particularly across the US, UK, and Middle East, where Tamil and Telugu films now routinely outperform Hindi releases on opening weekends. If DC works, it won't just prove Lokesh can act; it'll prove that a Tamil director's face alone can sell tickets — a genuinely new proposition for Indian cinema.

His dance card is, frankly, absurd. **Coolie** with **Rajinikanth** drops August 14 — barely two weeks after DC hits screens. After that, he moves to **AA23** with **Allu Arjun**, and then to the project everyone's really watching: a superhero action epic with **Aamir Khan**, which Lokesh has confirmed will target a global audience and is set to begin shooting later this year.

> "It is a Hindi film, but made for a global audience. I found a lot of similarities between Aamir sir and Kamal sir," Lokesh told The Hollywood Reporter India. "Our collaboration will bring about a new genre."

From Rajinikanth to Allu Arjun to Aamir Khan — Lokesh is collecting superstars the way other directors collect accolades. But first, he wants to prove he can be one.

**DC** opens in cinemas on **July 31** in Tamil, with wider release details pending. For NRIs across North America, the UK, and the Gulf, keep an eye on your local Tamil cinema listings. Anirudh, Matheswaran, and a gun-toting Devdas played by the man who built the LCU — this is one of those opening nights where you show up and find out if the director who orchestrates chaos can embody it too.

The Cannes trailer suggests he absolutely can.
